questions.q: What is a byte?
questions.explain: Computers store everything as bytes, numbers from 0 to 255. A character can take one byte or several, depending on the character and the encoding.
options: A number from 0 to 255; files and network messages are rows of bytes
A line of text ending in \n

questions.q: What is an encoding such as UTF-8?
questions.explain: An encoding maps characters to bytes and back. UTF-8 is the one used almost everywhere. It does not hide or compress anything.
options: A rule that says which bytes stand for which character
A way to hide text so only the owner can read it
A way to make a file smaller, like gzip
The name of the folder a file is saved in

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The string has 5 characters. In UTF-8, plain English letters take one byte each, but é takes two, so the buffer has 6 bytes.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Node.js prints each byte of a buffer in hexadecimal: 68 is h. Reading buf[0] gives the byte as a normal number, 104. toString("hex") writes the bytes as hex text.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A buffer works like an array of numbers. A is byte 65 and C is 67. (In hexadecimal they are 41 and 43, which is how console.log(buf) shows them.)
questions.code:
const buf = Buffer.from("ABC");
console.log(buf[0], buf[2], buf.length);

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: toString("base64") writes the bytes as base64 text. Buffer.from(encoded, "base64") reads that text back into the same bytes, and toString("utf8") turns them into the original words.

questions.q: A developer stores an API key in a config file as base64 and says "it is encrypted now". Is that right?
questions.explain: hex and base64 are ways to write bytes with safe, printable characters. They hide nothing: Buffer.from(text, "base64") gets the secret back. Keep secrets in environment variables, not in files.
options: No: base64 only writes bytes as printable characters; anyone can decode it in one line
Yes: base64 cannot be reversed without a key
Yes, as long as the base64 text ends with =
No, but hex would be encrypted

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ✅ is one character in JavaScript, but it takes three bytes in UTF-8. "ok " is three one-byte characters, so the total is 6 bytes.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The cut at byte 4 falls inside é, so each half decodes to the replacement character �. Join the bytes first with Buffer.concat, then decode, and the word is whole again.

questions.q: A program prints caf� instead of café. What most likely happened?
questions.explain: � means "these bytes are not valid text". UTF-8 stores é in two bytes; if a chunk ends between them, decoding each chunk alone breaks the character.
options: The bytes were cut in the middle of a character and each part was turned into text on its own
The file was saved with a Windows line ending
The text was too long for a buffer

questions.q: Why is readFile a bad choice for a 10 GB log file?
questions.explain: readFile holds all the data at once. A stream handles it chunk by chunk, so memory stays small whatever the file size.
options: It loads the whole file into memory at once, so the program can run out of memory
It can only read text files smaller than 10 MB
It changes the file while reading it

questions.q: Which kind of stream is gzip compression (createGzip())?
questions.explain: A transform is both writable and readable: you write the original bytes in and read compressed bytes out. That is why it sits in the middle of a pipeline.
options: A transform stream: data goes in, changed data comes out
It is not a stream; it is a function that returns a string

questions.q: In Node.js, process.stdout (where console.log writes) is which kind of stream?
questions.explain: You write data to process.stdout, so it is writable. That is why you can put it at the end of a pipeline.

questions.q: In an HTTP server, what kinds of stream are the incoming request and the response you send back?
questions.explain: The request body arrives piece by piece, so you read it. The response is something you write to. You will use both in the HTTP server lesson.
options: The request is readable; the response is writable
The request is writable; the response is readable
Neither is a stream; both are plain strings

questions.q: Inside a loop, out.write(line) returns false. What should your code do?
questions.explain: false means "my bucket is full, stop for a moment". The line was accepted; do not write it again. Wait for "drain", then carry on. This is backpressure.
options: Stop writing and wait for the "drain" event, for example with await once(out, "drain")
Write the same line again, because it was not saved
Throw an error: the disk is full

questions.q: What problem does backpressure solve?
questions.explain: If a loop keeps calling write faster than the disk saves, the waiting data grows in memory. Backpressure is the destination pushing back: write returns false until it has room again.
options: A writer that produces data faster than the destination can take it, so unsaved data piles up in memory
A file that is too big to fit on the disk
A reader that gets chunks in the wrong order
A stream that closes before it starts

questions.q: This writable stream holds at most 10 bytes before it asks you to wait. What does this print?
questions.explain: After the first write, 5 bytes are waiting, which is below the limit. After the second, 10 bytes are waiting, so write returns false. Once the stream has saved them, it emits "drain".

questions.q: You finished writing a file with a writable stream. What do out.end() and the "finish" event mean?
questions.explain: After end(), you may not write any more, but data may still be on its way to the disk. Wait for "finish" (for example await once(out, "finish")) before you rely on the file.
options: end() says "no more data"; "finish" says everything has been saved
end() deletes the file; "finish" says it is gone
end() and "finish" both mean the stream failed
end() saves the data; "finish" starts writing it

questions.q: What does once(out, "drain") from node:events give you?
questions.explain: once turns an event into a promise. await once(out, "drain") pauses your loop until the stream has room again.
options: A promise that resolves the next time out emits "drain", so you can await it
A listener that runs every time "drain" happens
The number of times "drain" has happened so far
A new stream that only emits "drain"

questions.q: You read a 7.7 MB file with for await (const chunk of createReadStream(file)). What is each chunk?
questions.explain: A file read stream gives Buffer chunks of up to 65,536 bytes. A chunk ends wherever 64 KB ends, not at the end of a line.
options: One line of the file, as a string
The whole file, as a string

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Readable.from turns each item of the array into one chunk, so the loop runs 3 times. Joining the chunks gives the full text back.

questions.q: Why should you not split each chunk with chunk.toString().split("\n") to read a file line by line?
questions.explain: Chunks are cut every 64 KB, wherever that falls. Lines get split in two and characters can break. readline's createInterface joins the pieces back into whole lines.
options: A chunk usually ends in the middle of a line, and can end in the middle of a character
split does not work on text that came from a file
It is correct, but slower than readFile

questions.q: The line breaks fall in the middle of the chunks. What does this print?
questions.explain: readline collects the chunks and gives you complete lines, without the \n, however the chunks were cut.

questions.q: What does crlfDelay: Infinity do in createInterface({ input, crlfDelay: Infinity })?
questions.explain: Windows ends lines with \r\n. This option makes sure readline sees those two characters as a single line break, even when they arrive in different chunks.
options: It makes a Windows line ending (\r\n) count as one line break
It waits forever for the file to finish
It reads the file with no memory limit

questions.q: Why does the lesson prefer pipeline from node:stream/promises over a.pipe(b)?
questions.explain: Both handle backpressure. But with .pipe(), a failing stream does not close the others or report the error in one place, so files stay open and errors go unnoticed.
options: When one stream fails, pipeline closes all of them and rejects one promise you can catch
.pipe() does not handle backpressure at all
pipeline reads the whole file into memory first, which is safer
.pipe() only works with text, not bytes

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first stream fails because the file is missing. pipeline closes the other streams and rejects with that error, so one try/catch covers the whole chain.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The transform gets each chunk and passes on a changed one with callback(null, newChunk). Each of the two chunks becomes an upper-case line ending in !.

questions.q: In a Transform, what is the first argument of callback(null, newChunk)?
questions.explain: Node.js callbacks put the error first. Pass null when all went well, or an Error to make the stream (and the pipeline) fail.
options: The chunk before it was changed
The name of the next stream

questions.q: A transform may pass nothing on. What does this print?
questions.explain: Calling callback(null, undefined) says "done with this chunk, nothing to pass on". So only the lines that contain done reach process.stdout.
options:
task 1 open
task 2 done
task 3 done

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Text that repeats a lot compresses well, so the gzip bytes are much smaller. Decompressing gives back exactly the original text; gzip loses nothing.

questions.q: The line-counting program uses about 5 MB of memory for a 7.7 MB file. About how much would it use for an 8 GB file?
questions.explain: That is the point of streams: memory depends on the chunk size, not on the size of the data.
options: About the same few megabytes, because it only holds one chunk and one line at a time
About 8 GB, because it must read the whole file
About 5 GB, a bit less than the file
It cannot read files bigger than 4 GB

questions.q: A hash can take its data in pieces. What does this print?
questions.explain: update can be called many times; the hash is the same as for the joined data. That is how you hash a huge file chunk by chunk with a stream.

questions.q: The build counts words with split(" ") and a filter. What does this print?
questions.explain: Two spaces in a row, and a space at the end, give empty strings when you split. Filtering out "" leaves the 3 real words.

questions.q: Data arrives in several Buffer chunks and you need the full text. What is the safe way?
questions.explain: Decoding each chunk alone can break a character that sits across two chunks. Joining the bytes first keeps every character whole.
options: Collect the chunks, join them with Buffer.concat, then call toString() once
Call toString() on each chunk and add the strings together
Convert each chunk to base64 and add the strings together
Read only the first chunk; the rest are copies

questions.q: Finish collectLines(chunks), a small version of what readline does. The chunks are strings that may end in the middle of a line. Return an array of the complete lines, without the \n. A last piece with no \n after it is also a line (if it is not empty).
questions.explain: Keep the unfinished end in rest. Add each new chunk to it, split on \n, and keep the last piece (which has no line break yet) for the next round. At the end, the leftover is the last line.

questions.q: Finish countLog(lines) like the build: count the lines, the words (split on spaces, ignoring empty strings), and the lines that contain " done ". The program should print {"lineCount":3,"wordCount":15,"doneCount":1}.
questions.explain: Loop over the lines once, keep three counters, and filter out the empty strings that double spaces create before counting words.

questions.q: Finish utf8Length(text), which counts how many bytes text takes in UTF-8, without using Buffer. Loop with for (const ch of text) and use ch.codePointAt(0): below 128 takes 1 byte, below 2048 takes 2, below 65536 takes 3, and anything bigger takes 4.
questions.explain: UTF-8 uses 1 byte for English letters and more bytes for other characters. for…of walks real characters, and the code point decides how many bytes each one needs.

questions.q: A file was read in chunks. Finish chunkStats(sizes), which gets the size of each chunk and returns how many chunks there were, the total bytes, and the biggest chunk. The program should print {"chunks":3,"bytes":140000,"biggest":65536}.
questions.explain: This is the same loop as the lesson's chunk reader: count, add the size, and keep the maximum with Math.max. Only one number per chunk is kept, never the data.

questions.q: The fake stream's write returns false when its bucket is full; stream.drain() empties it. Finish writeAll(stream, lines): write every line, and each time write returns false, call stream.drain() and count one pause. Return the number of pauses. The program should print 3 10.
questions.explain: Like the lesson's generator: if (!out.write(line)), wait for room (here drain()), then carry on. The line that returned false was still written, so do not write it again.

questions.q: How do you get Buffer in a Node.js program?
questions.explain: Buffer is built into Node.js and available everywhere, like console. It is not in the browser, which uses other tools for bytes.
options: It is global, so you use it without importing anything

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each line "task 1\n" is 7 bytes, so 3 lines are 21 bytes. After "finish" everything is saved, so reading the file finds all 3 lines.
